title: Quality, version control and delivery
subtitle: Keeping software good after the first release: quality assurance, version control, and pipelines that ship safely.

sections.title: Quality assurance
sections.body: Quality assurance (QA) prevents defects through process (standards, reviews, audits); quality control (QC) detects them (testing). Standards: ISO 9001, CMMI levels, ISO/IEC 25010 attributes. Reviews — inspections and walkthroughs — find defects earlier than tests.

sections.title: The cost of late bugs
sections.body: A defect costs roughly 1 unit to fix at requirements, ~10 in design/coding, ~100 after release. Hence reviews, static analysis and unit tests are worth their effort.

worked.why: A bug costing 1 h if found in requirements costs ~10× more in coding and ~100× after release.

choices.text: More work depends on the wrong decision.

problems.prompt: A project finds 60 defects in review and 20 in testing; 10 escape. Defect removal efficiency?

sections.title: Maintenance
sections.body: Four kinds: corrective (fix bugs), adaptive (new environment), perfective (new features/performance), preventive (refactor). Perfective is usually the largest share. Legacy systems are re-engineered or replaced when cost exceeds value.

sections.title: Version control and branching
sections.body: Configuration management tracks every version of every item. With Git: commit small changes, branch for features, merge via review. A common flow: main stays releasable; a feature branch is merged by pull request after tests pass.

choices.text: Review and automated checks before main changes.

sections.title: Continuous integration and delivery
sections.body: CI: every push is built and tested automatically. Continuous delivery: every passing build is deployable at a click; continuous deployment releases automatically. Small, frequent releases are easier to test and to roll back.

questions.prompt: In a CI pipeline a failing unit test should…

choices.text: Stop the pipeline and notify the author.

figures.caption: Figure 9.1.1 — CI/CD pipeline
figures.note: A failing stage stops the token; nothing after it runs.

sections.title: DevOps and recent trends
sections.body: DevOps joins development and operations: infrastructure as code, containers, monitoring, fast feedback. Other trends: microservices, cloud-native, AI-assisted coding (review its output like a junior’s), DevSecOps (security in the pipeline), low-code platforms.

worked.why: Deploy frequency rises from 1 per month to 1 per day.
That is about 30× more releases, each far smaller and easier to roll back.
